slides.headline: Heels lifting when you squat deep?
slides.sub: Your ankles might be the limit. Here's how to check and what helps.

slides.title: Ankles help set your depth
slides.body: As you squat, your knees need to travel forward over your toes. If your ankles don't bend enough, your heels lift, your chest tips forward or you stop short. It's a common, workable limit.

slides.title: Try the knee-to-wall test
slides.body: Kneel facing a wall with your front foot about a hand-width away. Keep the heel down and push your knee to touch the wall. Compare sides. A big difference between ankles is worth noting.

slides.title: Mobilise, then use it
slides.body: Rock your knee forward over your toes for 10 to 15 slow reps, heel down. Then go straight into a few squats so your body practises using the new range under load.

slides.title: Small tweaks while you build
slides.body: A slightly wider stance, toes turned out a touch, or a small plate under your heels can help you squat deeper while your ankle range builds over a few weeks.

slides.title: When to get it checked
slides.body: An ankle that has stayed stiff since an old sprain, a pinching pain at the front of the ankle when you squat, or swelling after training is worth an assessment rather than more stretching.

slides.headline: Want deeper, steadier squats?
slides.body: Our physios check your ankles, hips and squat pattern, then give you a short plan to build range you can actually use. Book online — link in bio.

caption:
Heels peeling off the floor at the bottom of your squat? Check your ankles before you blame your hips. 🏋️

Squatting deep needs your knees to travel forward over your toes, and that relies on ankle bend. When it runs short, your heels lift, your chest drops forward or you stop early.

Try the knee-to-wall test to compare sides, rock your knee forward for a few slow reps before you squat, and use a slightly wider stance or a small plate under your heels while your range builds. Pinching at the front of the ankle or a stiff ankle since an old sprain is worth getting assessed.
